# Book-level distillation — complete-chord-melody

_Aggregated from per-chapter summaries under `summaries/`._

This guitar method book is a structured, modular curriculum for learning jazz chord melody arranging and solo guitar performance, organized around a clear pedagogical arc: from foundational listening and conceptual orientation, through chord vocabulary and harmonization systems, to complete arrangement methodology, advanced substitution techniques, and finally the physical technique (fingerstyle mechanics) required to execute the arrangements. The book's spine is the chord melody tradition as practiced by masters like Joe Pass, Ted Greene, Lenny Breau, and Ed Bickert — players introduced in Chapter 1 and Chapter 2 not merely as inspirational figures but as exemplars of two distinct performance contexts the entire course is built around: solo guitar chord melody (unaccompanied) and trio chord melody (guitarist plus bass and drums). This solo/trio distinction is the book's primary structural lens, and the curriculum weight falls heavily on the solo context, which requires the guitarist to supply bass, harmony, and melody simultaneously.

The book's harmonic architecture is established in Chapter 3 and elaborated in Chapter 4. The foundational taxonomic system divides all chords into three primary families — Major, Minor, and Dominant — with Dominant subdivided into altered and natural sub-families, and Minor extended to include m7b5. This three-family framework is the theoretical backbone of the chord collection concept: a map of every diatonic interval above a given root so that any melody note can be correctly harmonized by selecting the chord voicing whose interval matches the melody note's relationship to the current chord. Chapter 4 establishes the 'golden rule' that governs all voicing selection: melody intervals must always be measured against the current chord in the progression, not against the overall key. This rule is presented as the central operating principle distinguishing correct from incorrect chord melody harmonization, and the CAGED system is the fretboard tool used to locate chord collections across the neck for melodies on both the first and second strings.

The book's core arrangement methodology is taught across Chapters 5 and 6 through a set of explicit, prescriptive rules. Chord placement should be sparse — applied only to long-held melody notes — because cluttering short notes destroys the melody's intelligibility. Shell voicings (root, 3rd, 7th) serve as the harmonic foundation because they state the chord's identity with maximum economy. The fifth, root, eleventh, and ninth may be omitted from voicings to maintain playability. When a melody note cannot sustain a chord, the rule is to substitute a chord voicing for the long note rather than abandon harmonization. A key philosophical stance runs throughout: difficult voicings are solved by cutting notes, not abandoning the chord, and arrangements succeed through implication and omission rather than completeness — the listener's mind completes a full-band texture from bass line plus sparse chords plus melodic line.

Walking bass is the structural engine of solo guitar arranging, detailed in Chapter 6 with its own rule set: root on beat 1, diatonic or chromatic approach note on beat 4, interior beats drawn from scales, chromatics, or arpeggios. Shell voicings drop onto the downbeat or the '& of 1' to maintain forward rhythmic drive. This walking bass-plus-shell-voicing framework defines the solo guitarist's functional role: the 5th and 6th strings carry the bass function that an upright bassist would supply in a trio, making low-string command non-negotiable. Chapter 6 also introduces the substitution vocabulary that constitutes the book's advanced harmonic language: tritone substitution (replacing any chord with one a tritone away, valid because guide tones swap positions while remaining common tones), relative substitution (vi for I), chord iii substitution, the minor-7-for-dominant rule (iim7 standing in for V7), and ii/V interchangeability — all techniques the book attributes to Joe Pass's characteristic style. The guide tone mechanism (the 3rd and 7th of each chord) is explicitly named as the harmonic engine underlying why substitutions work.

Joe Pass's defining moves appear throughout the book as the model for all characteristic technique. Chapter 3 introduces his signature horizontal-plus-vertical gesture: connecting block chord harmonizations with scalar passing tones, so that space created by long melody notes becomes room for linear single-note lines. Chapter 6 credits his liberal use of ii/V interchangeability and tritone substitution. Chapter 7 addresses his idiomatic use of rubato for dramatic phrasing effect. The book consistently presents Pass not as one option among many but as the primary exemplar whose practices define what 'authentic' jazz guitar arranging sounds and feels like — including the explicit statement that diads are preferred over octaves for a 'richer, more authentic' jazz sound.

Chapter 7 extends the substitution framework with back cycling (adding chords via the circle of fourths, with a caution against overuse in ensemble settings), common tone substitution (selecting substitute chords that share the current melody note), and lick swaps — replacing repeated melodic figures with idiomatic jazz licks matched to the harmonic context, reserved for later in the form to preserve listener orientation. The chapter also introduces the fifty-fifty principle: arrangement craft is only half of the performance equation, with execution — phrasing, touch, and rhythmic feel — constituting the other half. A specific rhythmic pitfall is named: solo guitar arrangements tend to drag behind the beat, producing a 'sleepy' feel; the prescribed remedy is progressive metronome training on beats 1-3 first, then 2-4.

The book's appendices (Chapters 8 and 9) deliver the physical technique layer, covering fingerstyle mechanics with the same rule-driven precision applied to harmony. The Spanish finger-naming convention (p, i, m, a, c) is established as the notation system for all subsequent exercises. Four wrist-placement rules govern injury prevention and tone production. Two plucking strokes are defined — rest stroke for initial learning, free stroke as the preferred jazz technique. The thumb's role is precisely specified: bass-note player only, motion originating from the lowest joint in a rowing-paddle action. Chapter 9 adds preferred finger pairings for adjacent and skip-string contexts, simultaneous note onset as the standard for clean chord plucking, and a standing mandate to vary finger combinations on repeated passages to expand picking vocabulary. The Moonwalker exercise, introduced in Chapter 8, exemplifies the book's pedagogical efficiency principle: consolidating two skills (walking finger alternation and string crossing) into a single exercise, mastered through five-minute daily sessions with measurable criteria before progression. Across both appendices, the master's characteristic pragmatism surfaces in legitimizing simplifications — thumb double-pluck, four-note voicing maximum, avoidance of the weak little finger — as deliberate professional choices rather than concessions to limitation.
